explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Paul writes, "We always thank God for all of you, remembering you in our prayers" (1 Thessalonians 1:2). That word is "always," which is a whole different thing from now and then. Now and then is how my old stamper handle got dusted, and this is the opposite of that.

That's right, friend. Paul says, "We always thank God for all of you, remembering you in our prayers" Always! Not once in a while, not when it's convenient. That's a team that keeps the thank-you going.

Yes, friend. Paul says it's their "…enduring hope in our Lord Jesus Christ." Notice that word enduring. It means this hope lasts, like an oven that holds its heat through the whole bake. And it has the right Person holding it up.

I see why a church might come to mind, since Paul is writing to one. But the verse puts their hope somewhere else, "…in our Lord Jesus Christ." Jerusalem doesn't come up in this passage at all. Their hope sits in a Person, friend, not a place.

Peter, the apostle, is a name you'd know, but he isn't in this passage. Paul says their enduring hope is "…in our Lord Jesus Christ." Hope that rests on a person like Peter would be shaky, because even the best of us have an off day. I know I have, and I once spent years behind a pile of takeout menus.

That's what the text says, friend. Paul writes, "Brothers who are beloved by God, we know that He has chosen you…" Beloved by God, and chosen. Sit with that for a second, because it's a lot of good news in one sentence.

This one is true, friend, so let's look at the verse. Paul says, "Brothers who are beloved by God, we know that He has chosen you…" He calls them beloved by God, and he says he knows they're chosen. It's all right there, plain as flour on an apron.

Yes, friend. Paul says the gospel came "…not only in word, but also in power, in the Holy Spirit, and with great conviction…" It wasn't just talk. Power, the Holy Spirit and great conviction all came along with the word.

Gold and silver would be shiny, I'll give you that. But Paul never mentions any treasure here. He says the gospel came "…in power, in the Holy Spirit, and with great conviction…" What they got was better than anything you could stack in a cookie box.

My own night sky does get a star every time a cookie box is finished, but that's the Dorinverse, not this verse. Paul doesn't say a word about the sky here. He says the gospel came "…not only in word, but also in power, in the Holy Spirit, and with great conviction…" So the answer is power and the Holy Spirit.

That's it, friend. Paul says they welcomed the message "…with the joy of the Holy Spirit, in spite of your great suffering." Joy and great suffering in the same sentence. That tells you this joy wasn't coming from easy days.
Wealth would make joy easier, wouldn't it? But the verse says "…in spite of your great suffering." The word "wealth" never shows up. Their joy came from the Holy Spirit, not from a fat bank account.

Doubt is a fair guess, since a new message can make anybody wonder. But Paul doesn't mention doubt here. He says they welcomed it "…with the joy of the Holy Spirit, in spite of your great suffering." So the word that fits is suffering.

Right, friend. Paul writes, "…you became imitators of us and of the Lord…" They watched how Paul's team lived and they followed. Same way my kitchen helpers learn to press clean and lift straight, by watching somebody do it first.
Rome is a long way from this verse. Paul says they "…became imitators of us and of the Lord…" The believers in Rome don't come up at all. The ones they imitated were Paul's team and the Lord.

Moses, Israel's leader, and the prophets are big names, but this verse doesn't use them. Paul says, "…you became imitators of us and of the Lord…" The "us" is Paul and his team, who lived among them. So the answer is Paul's team and the Lord.

That's the word, friend. Paul says, "…you have become an example to all the believers in Macedonia and Achaia." They went from learning to being the ones people learn from. That's a good day for any student.
An obstacle is something people trip over, and that isn't the word Paul picks. He says they became "…an example to all the believers in Macedonia and Achaia." The word he chose is example.

An outsider stands off to the side, and that isn't the word Paul picks. He says they "…have become an example to all the believers in Macedonia and Achaia." Outsider would be a very different thing to say about them. Paul's word is example.

Not quite, friend. Paul says the message of the Lord rang out from them to Macedonia and Achaia, and then he goes further: "…your faith in God has gone out to every place…" (1 Thessalonians 1:8). Every place! That's a lot bigger than two regions. It traveled farther than my cookie smell ever did, and that smell gets around.
That's right, friend. Paul says "…your faith in God has gone out to every place…" (1 Thessalonians 1:8). It didn't stay inside Macedonia and Achaia. It went well past them.

Yes, friend. Paul says their faith "…has gone out to every place, so that we have no need to say anything more." Their lives were already doing the talking. I'd love a cookie that advertised itself that well.

That's not what he says. Back in verse 2, Paul says they're remembering the Thessalonians in their prayers, and nothing here says that stops. What he says they have no need to do is "…say anything more." Their faith was already out there for everybody to see.

Paul doesn't say anything about writing again. The verse says their faith "…has gone out to every place, so that we have no need to say anything more." The thing he doesn't need to do is say anything more. Their faith was already doing the talking.
Right, friend. Paul says they "…turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God" Idols on one side, the living and true God on the other. That's a real turn, not a little nudge.
Trades sounds sensible, but Paul never says they left their work. The verse says they "…turned to God from idols…" It's idols they turned from, so the answer is idols.

Packing up and leaving town would be a big move, but this verse doesn't say it. Paul says they "…turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God" The turn was away from idols, not away from a place. So the answer is idols.
That's him, friend. Paul says they "…await His Son from heaven…" The Son is the One they're waiting on. And that's the very reason my ovens stay ready.

Elijah, a prophet of Israel, is a name that jumps out, so I get the pick, friend. But he never shows up in this letter. Paul says they "…await His Son from heaven…" (1 Thessalonians 1:10). So the Thessalonians have their eyes on the sky for God's Son, and nobody else is on their list.
Gabriel, an angel, is a big name, but he doesn't show up in this passage. Paul says they "…await His Son from heaven…" So it's God's Son they're waiting on, not an angel.

That's what the text says, friend. Paul says they await His Son from heaven, "…whom He raised from the dead…" God raised Him from the dead, and that's the Son they're waiting for. What a thing to look forward to.

Ha, this one is sneaky, friend, because the statement is true! Paul says they await His Son from heaven, "…whom He raised from the dead…" (1 Thessalonians 1:10). It's one Son, not two. The One they're waiting for is the very One God raised, so True was the pick here.
